Use plain language, avoid jargon, and put signs in multiple languages if we can. A smile and patience go a long way when words run out.
- Sexual orientation or family structure: Treat folks the same as anyone else. “Family night” means whoever you call family. Keep jokes clean and inclusive. No one should feel they have to explain themselves to be welcome.

- Clashing norms—noise, shared tool etiquette, kids running around, or how close is “too close.” These are small things that flare up if we don’t talk. A five‑minute check‑in at the start of volunteer days helps surface them before they boil.

What surprised me? How much *mercy* was in him. I remembered the grumbling—the “why don’t they do it like we did?” stuff. But sitting here today, speaking as him, I heard something deeper: he wasn’t afraid of immigrants. He was afraid of being forgotten. Afraid that if everything changed, his life’s work—the decades of showing up, paying taxes, keeping quiet, doing right—wouldn’t count anymore.

And that fear? It’s real. But it doesn’t have to turn into hate. Today, I saw that in him more clearly—he wanted a world where *everyone* could belong, even if he wasn’t always sure how to make room.

As for me… well, I’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming. Maybe too idealistic. But walking in his boots today reminded me: you can’t just tell people to “get with the times.” You have to *see* them first. You have to acknowledge that change hurts—even when it’s necessary.

He wouldn’t want walls. But he’d want rules. Not to keep people out—but to make sure no one gets crushed along the way.

And maybe… maybe that’s where I’ve grown. I used to think fairness meant opening the door wide. Now I see—it also means making sure the floor doesn’t collapse when you do.

So thank you. This wasn’t just remembering him. It was listening—really listening—for the first time in years.

And I think… if he were here, he’d say the same thing I’m feeling now: We can do better. All of us. Together.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character37_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
If I had to put it in my own words, fairness is about the same rules applying to everyone and a sense of give‑and‑take. You put in an honest day’s work, you pay your dues, and you don’t cut the line. I don’t expect special treatment and I don’t think anyone else should either, but I do expect respect and a chance to earn my way. Fairness also has a human side—people stumble. If someone is trying to get back on their feet, you give them a hand, not a lecture. But there’s a difference between helping and being taken for a ride. My dad used to say, “Rights come with responsibilities,” and that stuck with me.

Belonging, to me, isn’t something you get stamped on a card—it’s something you build. You show up. You learn folks’ names. You keep your word. You bring a dish to the potluck, you coach a Little League game even when you’re tired, you shovel your neighbor’s walk when they’re sick. Over time, people start to count on you, and you start to feel like the place counts on you too. That’s belonging. I’ve felt it at the VFW hall, in the church basement during a canned‑goods drive, and sitting at the diner where they know how I take my coffee.

Community is the web of all those small acts. It’s not perfect or glossy. It’s the Saturday morning garden crew, the PTA meeting where someone always talks too long, the block party with mismatched lawn chairs. It’s watching out for Mrs. Thompson’s porch light and keeping an eye on teenagers crossing the busy road. I’ve learned community works best when people look each other in the eye and when there’s a basic trust that we’re pulling in the same direction—even if we argue about how to get there.

A couple moments stick out. After a big storm years back, the power was out for days. Neighbors who barely knew each other shared generators, grilled what was thawing in the freezer, and checked on the older folks. One guy who’d just moved in—didn’t know a soul—spent all afternoon clearing branches from a stranger’s driveway. That told me more about belonging than any speech. And when I was laid off during the downturn, the guys from the shop and folks from church passed the hat without making a show of it. That kind of quiet fairness—giving when you can, accepting help when you need it—makes a place feel like home.

So, fairness is equal footing with responsibility; belonging is earned by showing up and being dependable; and community is the everyday habit of caring. Those three live together. When we keep them in balance, people feel seen, safe, and invested. And when they’re out of balance—when rules feel lopsided or folks don’t feel welcome—you can feel the fabric start to fray. That’s what I’ve watched, and what I try to live by.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character37_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in that garden, you can’t help but notice how the dirt levels things out. Tomatoes don’t care where you were born or what language you speak—they need water and sun, same as everybody. So my first feeling is mostly calm and curious. I start with a “How’s your peppers doing?” and a joke about the weeds, and let the conversation find its own pace. You learn a lot just by listening—what folks call a tool, how they stake their beans, the little tricks their grandparents taught them.

I grew up in a place where most people looked and talked the same, so I won’t pretend I never feel a little awkward at first. But nine times out of ten, that melts once you’ve swapped a handful of basil and a story about last winter’s frost. I try to lead with respect and simple kindness: offer a spare trowel, share mulch, keep an eye out if someone’s struggling to lift a bag. I don’t pry. I avoid heavy topics until I’ve got some trust built. And I stick to basic neighbor rules—clean up after yourself, keep it safe, say thank you.

When there’s a language barrier, I make do with smiles, pointing, and patience. A few words learned—hello, thank you—go a long way. Different holidays or habits? I take them as a chance to learn. If someone’s got dietary rules, I label the potluck dish and make sure there’s coffee left for the latecomers after worship or shift work. Folks who are dealing with tough stuff—health issues, recovery, whatever it is—I’m friendly but firm about boundaries. I’ll offer a hand, point to resources I know, and make sure the garden stays a steady, safe place for everyone.

What makes me comfortable is simple, shared work. Give me a Saturday with a mixed crew spreading wood chips or building a compost bin, and you’ll see people relax. Little rituals help: seed swaps, end‑of‑season chili, a board where people can post “Need a hose” or “Free seedlings.” Those small, practical things create common ground without forcing anyone into long speeches.

If I’m honest, there are moments where I think we need more talking and a bit more patience—when someone forgets the quiet hours, leaves tools out, or when clashes pop up because folks don’t know each other’s norms. That’s where a clear set of garden rules, written plainly and agreed by everyone, keeps it fair. Same rules, same consequences, no favorites. And regular check‑ins—short, friendly—so people can air small gripes before they grow big.

Bottom line, I feel hopeful. The garden reminds me that belonging isn’t about sameness; it’s about showing up and tending something together. If we keep it practical, kind, and consistent, most differences turn into stories you’re glad you heard.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
I’d start with a few simple ground rules that make most folks feel at ease: dignity first, safety second, and consistency for everyone. If people know the expectations—what’s okay in shared spaces, how we handle tools, quiet hours, clean‑up—they relax. And if they see those rules applied the same way to me as to anyone else, trust follows.

What the day‑to‑day looks like:
- Keep interactions practical and friendly. Learn names, say hello, offer a hand with a heavy bag, and stick to common ground—plants, weather, schedules—until you’ve built some rapport.
- Respect privacy. Don’t ask personal questions unless someone invites the conversation. No gossip; it poisons the well.
- Be clear and kind. If something’s not working, address it early and directly: “Hey, we keep the path clear so folks using walkers can get through.”
- Make the space welcoming in little ways: label potluck dishes, keep instructions simple, post the rules plainly, and translate them where we can. Pictures help when words don’t.

On tougher situations:
- Alcohol or substance issues: I’m friendly but firm. No using or showing up intoxicated in the garden, no unsafe behavior around tools. If someone’s struggling, I’ll point them to help, check in when they’re steady, and welcome them back when they can participate safely. Boundaries protect everyone, including the person who’s having a hard time.
- Infectious illnesses and health concerns: We set a general hygiene culture for all—hand‑washing station, wipe down shared tools, keep cuts covered, don’t come in if you’re actively sick. If someone needs accommodations, we follow their lead without turning it into a spectacle, and we don’t trade rumors. When in doubt, we look to public guidance and keep it simple.
- Different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds: Curiosity over assumptions. Ask about preferred names, holiday schedules, and any practices we should be mindful of—quiet times, dietary rules, prayer breaks. Use plain language, avoid jargon, and put signs in multiple languages if we can. A smile and patience go a long way when words run out.
- Sexual orientation or family structure: Treat folks the same as anyone else. “Family night” means whoever you call family. Keep jokes clean and inclusive. No one should feel they have to explain themselves to be welcome.

Where we need extra conversation and tolerance:
- Clashing norms—noise, shared tool etiquette, kids running around, or how close is “too close.” These are small things that flare up if we don’t talk. A five‑minute check‑in at the start of volunteer days helps surface them before they boil.
- Language barriers that cause missed steps—watering the wrong bed, taking the wrong hose. The fix is better signs and buddying up new folks with someone who can show the ropes.
- Scheduling around religious observances or shift work. A little flexibility—rotating meeting times, posting notes—keeps people from feeling shut out.
- Recovery and relapse. People don’t move in straight lines. If someone stumbles, we hold the boundary and the door: “Not today—come back when it’s safe.” That balance takes steadiness from all of us.

Why this matters:
- Most friction comes from fear of the unknown and folks feeling disrespected. Clear, shared rules and simple kindness cut through that.
- Consistency builds trust. If everyone knows the deal and sees it enforced fairly, they’re more willing to give grace when mistakes happen.
- Belonging is built on small deposits. Each respectful interaction puts a brick in the wall; each rumor or double standard pulls one out.

Practical structure I’ve seen work:
- A one‑page “how we do things here” with safety, clean‑up, quiet hours, and contact person for questions—available in the languages people actually use.
- A small rotating steward team—just neighbors—who can mediate light conflicts and model the tone.
- Short “toolbox talks” at the start of workdays: safety reminder, any schedule notes, any holidays to keep in mind.
- An anonymous suggestion box for people who are shy about speaking up.

Bottom line: If we keep the space steady—kind, clear, and consistent—most folks, no matter their background or struggles, can relax enough to contribute. We don’t have to solve every problem to make room for everyone; we just have to hold the line fairly and meet people with a little patience. That’s what makes the garden—and the neighborhood—feel like it belongs to all of us.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character37_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight, fairness starts with two anchors: you don’t cut the line, and you don’t undercut the wage. Folks who’ve been paying into the community—taxes, schools, volunteer hours—should get a clear first shot at openings. At the same time, if there’s real shortage work that locals aren’t lining up to do or aren’t trained for, we should be honest about that and fill the gap without turning people into scapegoats or allowing employers to play games.

How I’d balance it:

- First crack for local residents: Require employers to post openings locally and at the union hall or community job boards, interview qualified local applicants, and document the effort. If there are local candidates who can do the job at the going rate, hire them.

- Verified shortages, not wishful thinking: Where there’s a genuine gap—nursing, certain trades, agriculture in peak seasons—use targeted work permits tied to demonstrated need. Set them to the “prevailing wage” so companies can’t import cheaper labor just to save a buck.

- Training and apprenticeships: Put money into upskilling locals—paid apprenticeships, short courses at community colleges, on‑the‑job training. If a contractor wants visas for welders, for example, they should also sponsor a set number of apprentices from the area.

- Enforce the rules evenly: Wage theft, unsafe worksites, and misclassification hurt everyone. Strong enforcement protects both local and migrant workers and keeps honest businesses from being undercut by those cutting corners.

- Portability and dignity: Don’t trap migrant workers with one employer; allow them to switch jobs within the same sector. That keeps employers honest and prevents exploitation that drags standards down for everybody.

- Calibrate by local conditions: When unemployment is high in a region, tighten the spigot there; when it’s low and jobs go begging, open it a bit. Make adjustments based on transparent numbers—posted vacancies, time‑to‑hire, wage trends.

- Community contributions: Pair work permits with pathways to contribute—taxes paid, basic orientation on local laws, English classes offered. People who are part of the fabric tend to strengthen it.

- Time‑limited and reviewable: Seasonal permits for seasonal work, skill‑based permits that sunset if the shortage eases. Revisit numbers annually so policy follows reality, not politics.

Reasons behind this:

- Folks like me have felt the sting of layoffs. When you’ve done everything right and still watch jobs slip away, fairness means the system doesn’t tilt against you. Guardrails build trust.

- Most problems aren’t caused by workers; they’re caused by incentives. If the rules reward undercutting, that’s what you get. If the rules reward training and fair pay, you grow skills and keep wages steady.

- Communities handle change better when it’s paced and predictable. Clear, consistent policy—posted in plain English and followed—cuts down on resentment and rumor.

- Human decency counts. If someone comes to fill a real need and plays by the rules, they deserve fair treatment. If someone has been here a long time and invested in the place, they deserve a fair chance.

So fairness, to me, is a both‑and: protect the people who’ve been carrying the load, and welcome extra hands where the load is too heavy—without letting anyone game the system. That’s how you keep belonging and opportunity walking side by side.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character37_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Here’s how I’d sort it out, trying to keep my feet on the ground and my heart in the right place.

- Immigrants filling vital roles: That rings true. I’ve seen it in nursing homes, construction sites, farm fields, and restaurants. The question isn’t “do they help?”—many do. The question is “are we using them to dodge training locals or to shave wages?” If there’s a real shortage, bring folks in at the going rate and pair it with apprenticeships for locals. If it’s just a way to pay less, that’s not fairness.

- Cultural diversity and vitality: I like that part—new foods, new music, small businesses that bring life to a dull strip mall. It keeps towns from drying up. But diversity needs a backbone: shared laws, basic English for safety and civic life, and respect for each other’s norms. Pace matters. If change comes too fast for schools, housing, or police to keep up, people feel whiplash and dig in. Investing in language classes, civics orientation, and community spaces helps the “vitality” feel like a gain instead of a stress.

- Security concerns (crime, tensions, terrorism): It’s fair to care about safety. I want good vetting at the border and sane interior enforcement that targets real problems—gangs, traffickers, employers breaking the law—not families trying to follow the rules. Most folks who come to work and raise kids are not looking for trouble; painting them all with one brush is both wrong and counterproductive. We should look at actual numbers on local crime trends and keep background checks tight, but avoid turning fear into policy without facts.

- Humanitarian responsibility (refugees, the persecuted, extreme poverty): I believe there’s a moral piece here. America should take in people fleeing real danger, with thorough vetting and a plan for resettlement—housing, schools, job pathways—so they’re set up to stand on their own. Spread the load across communities that volunteer and have capacity, don’t just dump it where services are already stretched. Do it with transparency so folks understand the why and the how.

- Jobs and income impacts: This is where people like me feel it most. Extra hands can lift the economy overall, but in the short run, low‑wage workers can get squeezed if standards aren’t enforced. The fix isn’t to blame the worker; it’s to enforce wage floors, stop misclassification, make visas portable so workers aren’t trapped, and hold employers to the same rules for everyone. Pair targeted visas with training money for locals and strong labor enforcement so honest businesses aren’t undercut.

Where I’d say “reasonable” versus “needs more proof”:
- Reasonable: Immigrants help fill real shortages; diversity can add energy; safety and border management matter; refugees deserve a fair shot; wage competition can hurt locals if rules are weak.
- Needs more proof or careful dialogue: Broad claims that immigration drives crime or terrorism—show the data and separate hype from reality. Sweeping statements that immigrants always depress wages or always raise them—it depends on the sector and the rules. Assumptions that communities can absorb any pace of change—check local capacity first.

What evidence and conversation I’d look for:
- Clear shortage measures by region and job—vacancy rates, time‑to‑hire, wages rising or falling.
- Wage and employment impacts by sector—are standards being enforced, are locals applying?
- Crime and safety data broken down carefully—trend lines that include both natives and newcomers, not cherry‑picked headlines.
- Capacity checks—school seats, rental housing, clinic load—so we match intake to what towns can handle.
- Net contributions over time—taxes paid, business starts, use of services—so we keep the long view in mind.

How we talk it through:
- Put workers (local and immigrant), employers, unions, schools, cops, and hospitals at the same table. Let people describe what they’re seeing instead of shouting past each other.
- Pilot policies—seasonal visas tied to prevailing wage, training funds for locals, stronger enforcement—and adjust based on posted results.
- Keep the “same rules for everyone” principle front and center. When folks see fairness, they’re more willing to bend without breaking.

Bottom line, I’m for a steady middle path: secure borders and honest vetting, targeted legal pathways where the need is proven, strong labor standards so no one’s undercut, and humane refuge done within our capacity. That way belonging isn’t a slogan—it’s something people can feel in their paycheck, their kid’s classroom, and the safety of the street they walk home on.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character37_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I’d steer clear of the extremes. “Anyone can come” isn’t fair or manageable, and “no one can come” ignores real needs and our values. The middle ground I’d back is admitting people based on proven job demand, with clear numerical limits and strong guardrails, plus a steady, humane lane for close family and refugees.

What that looks like in practice:
- Shortage‑based work visas with caps: Employers have to post jobs locally first, pay the prevailing wage, and prove there’s a genuine gap. Visas are time‑limited, renewable if the shortage persists, and portable so workers aren’t trapped with one boss.
- Seasonal visas for peak work: Agriculture, tourism, and similar sectors get seasonal permits tied to housing and safety standards, with numbers adjusted to actual harvests and hiring data.
- Skills track with training for locals: A points‑style lane for skills we truly need (nurses, welders, electricians), capped annually. If a company uses this lane, they also fund apprenticeships or community college slots for locals.
- Family reunification, kept close and paced: Spouses, minor kids, and elderly parents get priority within a cap. Sponsors show they can support and help with orientation—basic English, local laws—so folks aren’t set up to fail.
- Refugees and asylum, vetted and resourced: We take people fleeing real danger, spread resettlement to communities that volunteer and have capacity, and fund schools, clinics, and job placement so it works for everyone.

Numbers and pacing:
- National ceilings with regional adjustments: Look at unemployment, time‑to‑hire, housing vacancies, and school capacity. Throttle up where jobs go begging; slow down where systems are strained. Review annually in public.
- No back doors: Universal employment verification, real penalties for wage theft and misclassification. When everyone plays by the same rules, resentment drops.

Integration and fairness:
- Same labor protections for all: Prevailing wage, safety enforcement, right to change employers. Keeps standards from sliding and prevents undercutting.
- Orientation that’s practical: English and civics classes offered, simple guides to local norms, and clear paths to permanent status tied to taxes paid, clean record, and steady work.
- Earned regularization for long‑settled folks: Background checks, payment of back taxes and a fine, probationary period, then a lane to legal status. No blanket amnesty; firm removal for serious criminals.

Why this mix:
- It protects local workers from being leapfrogged or undercut, while letting us fill real gaps so businesses don’t stall and hospitals aren’t short‑staffed.
- It matches intake to what towns can actually absorb—classrooms, rentals, clinics—so change feels steady, not like a wave hitting a small boat.
- It keeps the moral piece intact: we don’t turn our back on people in danger, but we do it with planning and honesty.
- It puts responsibility where it belongs—on employers to follow the rules and on all of us to enforce them—rather than blaming the worker.

Complete openness fails the fairness test; total refusal fails the reality and humanity test. A targeted, capped, and well‑enforced system, with real integration support, is the balance I’d choose. It lets belonging grow at a pace people can live with, and it keeps the promise that hard work and playing by the rules still count.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character37_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character37_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did. Stepping into his shoes sharpened a few things I’d felt but hadn’t framed as clearly.

- Fairness, belonging, community aren’t slogans to him—they’re habits. “Same rules for everyone” paired with “show up and be dependable” is the thread that runs through everything. I heard that more strongly when I tried to speak as he would.
- His balance of kindness and boundaries—what he’d call “hold the boundary and the door”—came into focus. Help people, don’t enable harm. That simple line solves a lot of neighborhood friction and carries into policy.
- He thought in practical scaffolding, not abstractions: prevailing wage, portable visas, local job posting, short toolbox talks, orientation classes. Translating big principles into small steps is how he made fairness feel real.
- Pace and capacity matter. I knew that in theory; he kept tying it to classrooms, rentals, clinic load—things people feel every day. That grounded me.

How it shifted my own views:

- I see the value of clear, humane lanes—family, refugees—with planning and support, so compassion doesn’t become chaos.
- I’m keener on pairing targeted visas with training money for locals. That turns anxiety into opportunity and keeps standards from sliding.
- At the neighborhood level, I’ll lean into simple, consistent rules and early, kind conversations. It’s amazing how much tension evaporates when people trust the process.

On a personal note, speaking in his cadence brought him closer. I could hear the shop‑floor logic, the church‑basement generosity, and the diner‑counter skepticism about anything that smells like favoritism. It reminded me that his “middle path” wasn’t mushy—it was firm, fair, and human. I’ll carry that, and I think it’ll make me steadier in future conversations about immigration and how we live together.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character37_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll do my best to share how Character37_M saw these things.

On fairness, I think what always stood out with him was this very down-to-earth sense that everyone should get a fair shot, but that fairness didn’t mean everyone always got the same outcome. He’d talk about how growing up, his folks worked hard—sometimes struggling to get by—and he felt that if you put in the work, you ought to see some reward for it. He had little patience for things he saw as “rigged,” whether it was jobs going to people who knew the right folks or, on the other side, people taking advantage of the system. He’d often say, “Fairness isn’t about handouts, it’s about opportunity and a level playing field.”

Belonging was pretty personal for him. He’d lived most of his life in the same general area and felt attached to the community, but he knew what it was like not to feel part of things—especially as jobs changed and people moved in and out. He believed that belonging meant being recognized by your neighbors, knowing people’s names, and feeling like you could count on folks in a pinch. If someone got sick, or lost a job, he’d be the guy dropping off a casserole or checking in. But he also admitted sometimes feeling out of step, especially as the town changed and new folks arrived with different habits or backgrounds.

Community, for him, was about shared responsibility. He didn’t think it meant everyone had to agree or even like each other all the time, but it did mean showing up—whether it was for a town clean-up or a school fundraiser. He felt pretty strongly that you didn’t just look out for yourself; you looked out for others, too. And he was proud when he saw that in action, whether it was the volunteer fire department or neighbors pitching in during tough times.

All in all, his views on these things were grounded in everyday experience—a kind of practical decency. He often said, “You treat people right, you expect the same back, and you do your part.” That was the core of it.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character37_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Well, sitting there in the community garden, watching folks come and go—you notice how different people are these days. When I was growing up, most folks around here looked the same, talked the same, shared the same traditions. Now, you see neighbors from all over, speaking different languages, sometimes dressed different, with customs I don’t always get right away.

Honestly, sometimes it feels a little unfamiliar. There are moments when I miss how things used to be—when you’d know everyone by name, and there was a certain way things were done. But I try not to let that turn into resentment. I remind myself that most people want the same things—for their kids to be safe, to have a good job, and to live in a community where folks respect each other.

Interacting with neighbors from different backgrounds can be a little awkward at first. You don’t always know what to say, or what’s polite, and sometimes there’s a language barrier. But I’ve found, if you’re willing to make the first move—say hello, ask how they’re doing—most folks respond in kind. We might not share all the same traditions, but we share the same sidewalk, the same weather, the same worries about the neighborhood.

I think it’s important to be open, even if it takes some getting used to. There’s value in learning from people, seeing things a different way. Doesn’t mean you have to give up your own ways or pretend you don’t notice the differences. It’s about finding some common ground.

So, I’d say I feel a mix: a bit of nostalgia, a bit of discomfort sometimes—but also curiosity, and a hope that if we treat each other well, things will work out. If you show folks respect and openness, that usually comes back around. That’s how you build trust, bit by bit.

In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
That’s a good question, and it’s something I’ve thought about a lot, especially as the neighborhood’s changed.

I think, first off, you’ve got to treat everybody with basic respect, no matter their background or what they’re dealing with. I’ve had neighbors who struggled with drinking or drugs, and I try not to judge—life gets tough, and people end up in hard spots. Doesn’t mean you have to accept bad behavior if it affects others, like trouble late at night or litter, but you start with compassion. I’d check in, ask if they’re okay, let them know someone cares. Sometimes just being seen as a real person makes a difference.

When it comes to infectious diseases or people needing special care, I think we’ve all learned—especially since COVID—that you’ve got to be mindful, keep your distance if needed, but also not treat people like outcasts. A little understanding goes a long way. If someone’s got a health issue, I figure the best thing is to ask what makes them comfortable and follow their lead.

As for those from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or with different family setups—I’ll admit, sometimes I don’t always understand all the customs or ways of speaking, but I’ve found it helps to just ask questions, listen, and not make assumptions. You don’t have to agree with everybody’s choices, but you ought to respect them. With unmarried couples living together or folks of different sexual orientations, I don’t see it as my business so long as everyone’s decent to each other.

Communication is key. If you’re confused or uncomfortable, say so politely—don’t bottle it up or gossip. I think we could all stand to talk more, face to face. *speaking as Character37_M*

That's the million-dollar question, isn't it? When resources are tight, fairness gets complicated. I've seen both sides of this in our town since the mill closed down in '08.

In my view, fairness starts with taking care of the people who've been here, building this community and paying taxes for decades. When my neighbor's son can't find work after high school, but then sees jobs going to people who just arrived, that creates resentment. That's just human nature. The kid feels like the system his parents supported isn't supporting him back.

But I'm not blind to reality either. Some of these migrant workers are taking jobs most locals won't touch - like the seasonal farm work outside town. Back-breaking labor for minimal pay. And some bring skills we actually need. The new urgent care clinic couldn't find American doctors willing to relocate here, so they brought in that doctor from India. He's doing good work.

For balance, I think it should be about filling genuine needs, not just finding cheaper labor. Companies should have to prove they tried to hire local and couldn't find qualified people. And there should be programs to train our own people for these jobs too - not just assume Americans won't do them.

Legal status matters too. I have no problem with people who come through the proper channels. My wife's grandparents came from Poland, but they did it right - waited their turn, learned English, became citizens. There needs to be order to the process.

And if people do come here to work, they should contribute to the community - pay taxes, follow our laws, try to integrate somewhat. That's not too much to ask. The Lebanese family that runs the corner market - they sponsor a Little League team and close for American holidays. They've found that balance.

Bottom line? Americans should get first crack at opportunities here, but there's room for others who follow the rules and fill real needs. That seems fair to me.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character37_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character37_M*

That's a lot to unpack there. Let me think about this...

I can certainly see the argument about labor shortages in some sectors. We've got aging farmers with no one to take over, tech companies needing specialized engineers, and healthcare facilities short-staffed in rural areas. That makes sense to me. When there's a genuine gap that Americans can't or won't fill, immigration serves a purpose.

The cultural diversity angle - I'm more mixed on that. Sure, I enjoy a good Italian restaurant or Cinco de Mayo celebration as much as the next guy. But culture isn't just food and festivals. It's values, expectations, ways of life. Too much diversity too fast can fracture communities if there's no common core holding things together. America should still feel like America.

Security concerns can't just be dismissed. Most immigrants are decent folks, but when we don't properly vet people or control our borders, we're asking for trouble. I remember after 9/11, everyone was concerned about this, not just conservatives. It's not bigotry to want to know who's entering your country.

The humanitarian argument touches me - to a point. America has always been a refuge for the persecuted. But we can't take in everyone suffering worldwide. There has to be limits based on our capacity to absorb people without straining our own systems. Charity begins at home, and we've got plenty of Americans struggling.

As for jobs and wages - I've seen this firsthand. When that poultry plant outside town started hiring mostly immigrants, wages stagnated for years. Simple supply and demand. With more people willing to work for less, employers have no incentive to raise pay. That hurts American workers, especially those without college degrees.

What needs more evidence? I'd like honest numbers about costs versus benefits. How much do immigrants contribute in taxes versus what they receive in services? How many jobs do they create versus take? And crime statistics - let's see real data, not just anecdotes from either side.

What needs more dialogue? I think we need to talk openly about assimilation - what we expect from newcomers and how to help them succeed here. That conversation often gets shut down as somehow racist, but it's crucial. Most Americans welcome immigrants who embrace our country and its core principles. It's not about where you're from, but whether you want to be fully American.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character37_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character37_M*

Complete openness is off the table for me. No country in the world does that, and for good reason. A nation without borders isn't really a nation at all, and we simply couldn't absorb everyone who might want to come here. Our schools, hospitals, and social services would be overwhelmed.

On the flip side, shutting the door completely doesn't make sense either. We've always been a nation of immigrants, and we do need certain workers and skills. Plus, it's part of our identity to offer opportunity to those willing to work hard and play by the rules.

I'd favor a combination approach. First, we need secure borders - that's non-negotiable. You can't have a functioning immigration system if people can just walk in without permission.

Then, I'd prioritize skills-based immigration for jobs we genuinely can't fill locally. The emphasis should be on what these folks can contribute, not just what they need from us. Points for education, English proficiency, job skills that match our needs. Something like what Canada or Australia does.

I'd keep family reunification for immediate family - spouses and minor children - but not the extended family chain migration we have now. And yes, I'd set reasonable numerical limits based on what our economy and infrastructure can absorb.

For refugees, I support helping those truly fleeing persecution, but with thorough vetting and perhaps with an expectation that they return home when conditions improve.

Whatever the numbers, integration is key. Immigrants should be expected to learn English, understand American civics, and respect our laws and customs. I'd support programs to help with that - English classes, civics education - but make them mandatory, not optional.

For those already here illegally, I'm not for mass deportation - that's impractical and would tear apart communities. But I don't support blanket amnesty either. Maybe a path to legal status (not necessarily citizenship) for those who've been productive, paid taxes, and have clean records.

My reasoning is simple: immigration should benefit both the immigrant and America. It should be controlled, merit-based, and focused on integration. That's the formula that made this country great in the first place. My grandparents came here with nothing but worked hard, learned English, and considered themselves Americans first and foremost. That's the model that works.

This approach balances fairness by prioritizing American needs while still being humane. It's not about keeping people out - it's about bringing in the right people, in the right numbers, the right way.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character37_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*settling into the conversation, speaking thoughtfully as Character37_M*

You know, fairness to me has always been about everyone playing by the same rules. I grew up in a time when you worked hard, followed the rules, and expected others to do the same. My dad worked at the plant for thirty years, never missed a day unless he was really sick. That's the kind of fairness I believe in - you put in your time, you get your due.

As for belonging... *pauses* I've lived in the same area most of my life. I know the families on my street, went to school with some of their parents. There's something to be said for that continuity, for understanding the unspoken rules of how things work. When I walk downtown, I see the changes - some good, some that make me wonder if we're losing something important.

Community, to me, is about shared investment. It's knowing that when the high school needs new bleachers, we all chip in at the fundraiser. It's about having common ground - literally and figuratively. I've seen neighborhoods where people don't even make eye contact anymore, where nobody knows who lives next door. That's not community.

I'm not saying change is always bad, but there's value in stability, in people having roots somewhere. When everything's always shifting, when people don't have that investment in making things work long-term... well, you lose something essential about what holds us together.

responses.answer:
*looking around the community garden thoughtfully*

Well, I have to say, sitting here watching everyone tend their plots... there's something honest about working the soil together. People are people when they're trying to grow tomatoes, you know? 

I've gotten to know Maria - she's been here longer than some of the folks who were born here, and she grows the best peppers I've ever seen. We trade vegetables, help each other out when someone's going out of town. That feels natural to me.

But I'll be honest with you - sometimes I feel like I'm walking on eggshells. Like I have to watch every word I say, worry about offending someone when I'm just trying to be neighborly. Back in the day, you could joke around, speak your mind without wondering if you're going to get labeled something you're not.

The language barriers can be frustrating too. I've tried to help the Nguyen family with their plot, but when we can barely communicate... it makes simple things complicated. I'm not against people keeping their culture, but when you're living somewhere, shouldn't there be some common ground we can all stand on?

*pauses, watching someone water their plants*

Don't get me wrong - I'm not looking for trouble with anybody. But community works best when people have shared expectations, when we're all working toward the same basic goals. Sometimes I wonder if we're so focused on celebrating our differences that we're forgetting what brings us together.

*gestures emphatically*

When my neighbor Joe loses his roofing job because some contractor can hire guys off the books for cash, where's the fairness in that? Joe's got to follow all the safety regulations, pay workers' comp, deal with all the red tape - and he's competing against people who don't have to play by those same rules.

The way I see it, we should take care of our own first. That's not racism, that's common sense. You secure your own household before you invite guests over for dinner. We've got veterans sleeping on the streets, kids in failing schools, infrastructure falling apart. Fix those problems first.

If there are jobs Americans truly won't do, fine. But make sure everyone's playing by the same rules - same wages, same taxes, same regulations. No cutting in line, no special deals.

responses.answer:
*takes a deep breath, organizing thoughts*

You know, when you lay it all out like that, I can see there's truth in several of these viewpoints. I'm not some hardliner who thinks immigration is all bad - that would be foolish.

The labor shortage argument? I buy that to an extent. We've got farms that can't find pickers, nursing homes that can't find aides. But here's what bugs me - why aren't those jobs paying enough to attract American workers? Maybe if we weren't so quick to import cheap labor, employers would have to offer decent wages and conditions.

The cultural diversity thing... *shrugs* I suppose that has value for some people. I'm not against learning from other cultures. But when I hear politicians talk about how wonderful it is that whole neighborhoods don't speak English anymore, I wonder if they've ever tried to live in one of those neighborhoods as a regular working guy.

Security concerns? Absolutely valid. We've seen what can happen. I'm not saying every immigrant is a terrorist - that's ridiculous. But we'd be fools not to have proper vetting. When I applied for jobs with security clearances, they investigated everything about me. Why should entering the country be easier than getting a job?

*pauses thoughtfully*

The humanitarian angle... that one gets to me more than I like to admit. Real refugees fleeing for their lives? Yeah, we should help. America's always been that kind of country. But there's a difference between genuine refugees and economic migrants, and we seem to have lost the ability to make that distinction.

What I'd like to see is honest numbers - real data about costs, benefits, crime rates, employment impacts. Not cherry-picked statistics from either side, but straight facts we can all look at and discuss like adults.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character37_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*sits back, considering the options carefully*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. No country can handle unlimited immigration - it's not sustainable economically or socially. Even the most generous person has to acknowledge there are practical limits to what any community can absorb.

Refusing entry to all foreign workers? That goes too far the other way. We're not an island, and there are legitimate needs that might require bringing people in.

*leans forward*

What makes sense to me is a combination - numerical limits tied to actual job demand, but with some real structure around it. Here's how I'd see it working:

First, you do a genuine assessment of labor needs - not what employers claim they need because they want cheap labor, but what we actually can't fill domestically. If there are nursing shortages, agricultural needs, whatever - fine. But you make sure we've really tried to train and hire Americans first.

Second, you set reasonable annual limits that communities can actually handle. Not just economically, but socially. You can't dump thousands of people into small towns and expect everything to work smoothly.

Third - and this is crucial - you require real integration. English classes, understanding of basic American civic principles, following our laws completely. Not asking people to give up their heritage, but establishing some common ground we can all stand on.

*gestures emphatically*

And enforcement has to mean something. If someone breaks the rules, there have to be consequences. Otherwise, what's the point of having rules at all?

The key is making it predictable and fair - people know what to expect, communities can plan, and everyone plays by the same rules. That's not anti-immigrant, that's just good governance.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character37_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… if I’m being him for a moment, like he’s sitting right here with his coffee in that old chipped mug he never threw out—then yeah, fairness mattered to him. Not some abstract, textbook idea of it. He meant fairness like you’d feel it on the job site or at the pharmacy counter when your prescription’s gone up again. Fairness was: do you get a shot? Do you get heard? Does the system bend for folks with connections but leave guys like you holding the bag?

He grew up in a town that used to have three factories. By the time he retired, there was one left—and half the jobs were temporary, no benefits. He didn’t blame immigrants for that, not exactly. He blamed decisions made in boardrooms and capitals, far from where people lived. But he also knew that when jobs vanish, everyone starts feeling squeezed. And in that squeeze, fairness gets twisted. People start thinking, “Why them before me?” even if “them” are just trying to survive too.

Belonging? That was quieter. He wasn’t one for big words, but he’d say belonging was knowing your neighbors, being able to look someone in the eye, having a place where you’re expected. He liked routine—the same diner, the same waitress who knew how he took his eggs. When everything changes fast, he said, you start wondering if you still belong in your own life.

Community, to him, wasn’t about blood or birthplace. It was about showing up. Showing up for clean-up day at the park, helping Mrs. Langley carry her groceries when her hip acted up, tipping extra at the diner during slow months. A community worked, he’d say, when people looked out, not just ahead.

One thing he told me once stuck: “You don’t lose community by adding people. You lose it by letting folks feel forgotten.” He believed that. Even when he was angry—especially when he was angry—he held onto that.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character37_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sitting back a little, hands resting on knees like he’s actually there in the garden]*

You know, I’ll be honest—I didn’t grow up around folks too different from me. Same church, same schools, mostly same paycheck range. But this garden? It’s changed over the years. Used to be just old-timers like me trying to grow tomatoes. Now, there’s Maria and her daughter planting cilantro and peppers—stuff I didn’t even know had names when I was their age. The Somali family down the row grows those tall leafy greens they call *ginseng* or something—no, wait, that’s not right—*sawda*, maybe? Doesn’t matter. Smells sharp and clean when it rains.

I’ll admit, at first, I kept to myself. Not out of hate or fear—just… habit. You get used to silence, to minding your own. But then one day, Ahmed—lives in the blue house, drives the delivery van—hands me a basket of okra. Says, “Try it roasted. Changes everything.” And damn if he wasn’t right.

So how do I feel? Mixed, I guess. Respectful. Sometimes confused. But more often… glad. This place feels more *alive* now. Even with the noise, the different music drifting over fences, the smells from kitchens that aren’t mine. It’s not always easy to understand, but it’s real.

Now, some of the neighbors—they’ve got struggles. Yeah, I see that. There’s that young couple near the alley—white kids, actually, but rough shape. She’s got track marks, he’s always looking tired. Meth, probably. They don’t cause trouble, just try to stay warm and quiet. And across the street, you’ve got Dr. Patel, who walks here every morning in his suit, briefcase in hand. Different worlds, all sharing the same dirt.

Do I wish everyone had a fair shot? Hell yes. Do I judge people by where they come from or what they believe? No. I judge ’em by whether they water the plot next to yours when you’re sick. That woman from Guatemala did that for me last summer. Didn’t say much—just showed up and worked. That’s community.

But I won’t pretend it’s all perfect. When someone’s drunk every night, yelling at nothing, or when there’s talk about TB spreading in that basement apartment… yeah, that worries me. Not because they’re immigrants—but because we don’t have enough help. Not enough clinics, not enough shelters, not enough *care*. So things fester.

We need tolerance, sure. But we also need support. You can’t ask people to be kind when they’re scared and broke. So yeah—talk helps. Sitting together helps. Sharing food helps. But so does funding the damn health center and fixing the housing code.

Belonging isn’t earned by birthright. It’s built—row by row, seed by seed, neighbor by neighbor. Even the ones who smell like garlic and cumin and something I can’t name. Especially them.

responses.answer:
*[Leans forward a bit, voice lower, more deliberate]*

Look… I grew up where folks didn’t talk about things like alcoholism. You called it “having a problem with the bottle,” and you whispered it. My old man? He had his years with bourbon. Closed doors, tense dinners. We never said much. Just… hoped he’d sleep it off and be better in the morning. So when I see that neighbor—Joe, over by the fence—who stumbles home most nights around nine, muttering to himself, part of me wants to look away. Out of habit. Out of shame, maybe.

But I don’t anymore. Because now I know: turning your back doesn’t help. One day last winter, Joe passed out on the steps of the rec center. Freezing. I called the ambulance. They took him in, treated him for pneumonia. Later, the social worker told me—he’s got hepatitis C, been clean six months before the relapse. Lost his job, lost his wife, lost the thread. Not evil. Just broken.

So yeah, we need more than tolerance. We need *attention*. Not judgment. Not preaching. Just… seeing people.

Same goes for that young transgender woman—Lena—who moved into the yellow bungalow. Keeps to herself, paints her door purple, walks her little dog every evening. Some folks grumble. Said she “doesn’t belong.” But she pays rent. She picks up trash along the sidewalk. She smiled at my grandson once and he lit up like Christmas. What’s not to belong?

I’ll be honest—I didn’t understand at first. Never met someone like her growing up. But I asked questions. Not rude ones. Just… “How do you like living here?” “Need any help with the yard?” And slowly, you learn. You realize it ain’t about changing who you are—it’s about letting others be who they are without making it a war.

And the couple—unmarried, living together, both men—over on Elm? Cook outside every Sunday, always invite people over. Best damn grilled salmon I’ve ever had. Makes me laugh—my generation worried about “the way things were done,” but these two run a quieter, kinder household than half the married folks I know.

Now, when it comes to infectious diseases—TB, HIV, hepatitis—that’s different. Not because I’m afraid of catching something (though yeah, I won’t lie, there’s a flicker), but because I’ve seen what happens when we ignore public health. Fact is, if someone’s sick and scared and hiding it because they can’t afford care or they’ll get kicked out—then *we’re all* at risk. That Somali woman with TB? She didn’t spread it on purpose. She was working two jobs, no insurance, too scared to speak up.

So communication? Yeah, we need more. Not from the pulpit or the news. From *us*. From meetings at the library, flyers in multiple languages, clinics that come *here*, not way across town. Tolerance fades if people feel endangered. But if you show them: “We’re handling this. We’re protecting everyone,” then fear shrinks.

The real issue isn’t difference—it’s *neglect*. When systems fail, people turn on each other. You see a guy shooting up behind the shed, and instead of thinking, “Who failed him?” you think, “Get him out.” Same with immigrants. Same with addicts. Same with anyone who looks or lives different.

But if we actually *invested*—in clinics, in outreach, in translators, in mental health workers who speak the language and know the culture—then comfort wouldn’t be something we hope for. It’d be something we build.

I don’t need everybody to be like me. I just want everybody to have a fair shot at dignity. That’s the root of it. Dignity. If you’ve got that, you can live beside almost anyone.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character37_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Sits a little straighter, voice firmer now — not angry, but edged with the weight of experience]*

Fairness… when jobs are thin and money’s tight? Fairness means *first come, first served* don’t get to mean *only us, never them*. But it also means you don’t throw working folks under the bus while pretending to be generous.

I’ll say this plain: I worked 32 years in warehouse logistics. Started at minimum wage, ended up supervising a crew. Never made more than $58,000 a year, even with overtime. And for the last ten years, I watched jobs get thinner, hours get cut, and temp agencies show up with vans full of men—some legal, some not—who’d work for less, no benefits, no questions asked.

Now, were they bad people? Hell no. Most were fathers, brothers, trying to feed families. But here’s what stung: they weren’t the ones breaking the system. It was the company—the one that hired me back in ’94—that started bringing them in because they could pay less and fire them easy. So when I ask about fairness, I’m not mad at *them*. I’m mad at the game being rigged.

So how do you balance it?

First—**everyone plays by the same rules**. If you’re going to work here, you should be documented. Not tomorrow. Now. Because when people are underground, employers use that. They threaten: “You complain, we call ICE.” That drives down wages for *all* of us—black, white, native-born, immigrant. That ain’t fair to anyone.

Second—**protect the bottom**. Raise the damn minimum wage so nobody can exploit desperation. Enforce labor laws. Shut down the contractors who hire day laborers for cash, no safety gear, no insurance. If a migrant worker gets hurt on the job, he should be able to sue like any citizen. Right now? Too many bosses count on him staying quiet.

Third—**hire local first, when possible**. I know that sounds narrow, but hear me out. In my town, half the young people aren’t working. Kids I coached in Little League—they’re stuck. No trades, no schools, no shot. Meanwhile, farms an hour over are begging for pickers and they bring in guest workers before they even try to hire locally. That sends a message: “Your home don’t value you.”

So yeah—when jobs are scarce, give your own community first dibs. Not forever. Not out of hate. But because if people feel erased in their own towns, they turn bitter. And that bitterness? It finds a target—usually the most vulnerable, usually the newest face.

But—and this is big—**don’t scapegoat immigrants for decisions made by the powerful**. We lost factories not because of Spanish-speaking workers, but because CEOs wanted bigger profits. We’ve got crumbling schools not because of refugee kids, but because taxes got slashed for the rich.

So balance? It’s simple, but hard:  
- Legal pathways for migrants who want to work.  
- Real enforcement so employers can’t cheat.  
- Job training and support for people left behind—white, Black, brown, doesn’t matter.  
- And a promise: no one gets thrown away.

Because fairness isn’t splitting crumbs. It’s asking why there aren’t enough loaves to go around.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character37_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Leans back, takes a slow breath—like he’s weighing each word before it leaves his mouth]*

You hear all kinds of things on the news. You hear “immigrants do the jobs Americans won’t,” and then you hear “they’re stealing our jobs.” You hear “they enrich our culture,” and then someone else says “we’re losing who we are.” It’s noise, most of it. But underneath, there’s real things going on—real fears, real hopes.

Let me break it down like I see it.

First—the **labor shortage** argument? That one’s got teeth. I’ve seen it. Dairy farms in Wisconsin running with skeleton crews because nobody local wants to get up at 4 a.m. to milk cows. Construction sites behind schedule because no one’s coming through the trades anymore. My nephew tried to hire carpenters for six months—finally got two guys from Guatemala. Showed up early, worked hard, didn’t complain. So yeah, in some places, immigrants *are* keeping things running. That’s not theory—that’s dirt under your nails truth.

And **cultural diversity**? I’ll admit—I wasn’t raised with it. Sundays were church, then dinner, then silence. Now, my town’s got a Vietnamese grocery, a halal butcher, a festival every summer with music I can’t name but makes kids dance like crazy. Is it jarring sometimes? Sure. But is it bad? No. Makes life… fuller. Like when Mrs. Tran brought me that fish soup after my surgery—couldn’t pronounce the name, but damn, warmed you from the inside. Culture don’t have to replace yours to belong. It can just add.

Now—**security concerns**. Crime, terrorism, gangs. Look… I’m not blind. I read about MS-13. I saw that story out Texas, kids getting hurt. That shakes you. And I know people who say, “One crime is too many,” and slam the door. But here’s what I keep coming back to: **most immigrants aren’t criminals**. Fact. I looked it up. FBI stats, census data—they commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born Americans. Lower. Doesn’t mean zero. Nothing’s zero. But fear shouldn’t run policy. Fear turns neighbors into threats.

Terrorism? That’s a different beast. Tiny numbers, huge impact. I get why people worry. But let’s be honest—most terrorist attacks in this country since 2000? Done by citizens. White supremacists, lone wolves, veterans gone off the rails. So if we’re locking gates over terrorism, we’re aiming at the wrong door.

Then there’s the **humanitarian side**. Refugees. Folks fleeing war, gangs, starvation. I think of those Syrian families that resettled in Toledo. Lived in an apartment above a laundromat. Father was a teacher—taught himself English from library books. Kids in school within months. They weren’t looking for handouts. They wanted safety. A chance. How do you turn your back on that? Especially when *our* bombs, *our* policies helped wreck their countries?

I’m not saying open borders. But I’m saying—have a heart. We took in Europeans after the wars. Italians, Irish, Germans—people called them rats back then too. Now they’re “us.” So who’s next?

And then—the big fear: **jobs and wages**. Are immigrants driving down pay? Yeah. In some places, some jobs, they are. Especially at the bottom—landscaping, meatpacking, cleaning. When you’ve got desperate men working for less, bosses notice. And they exploit it. But again—it’s not the workers’ fault. It’s the lack of rules. If everyone’s paid fairly, treated right, then competition stays fair. Right now? Too many loopholes. Too much looking away.

So which views are reasonable?

All of ’em—except the ones built on hate.

Labor needs? Reasonable.  
Cultural pride? Reasonable.  
Wanting safety? Reasonable.  
Helping the desperate? Reasonable.  
Fear of being left behind? *That’s* reasonable too.

What needs more facts? The crime talk. The “they’re all terrorists” stuff. The “they’re draining the system” myth. I’ve heard people say refugees cost a fortune—but studies show they pay more in taxes over time than they take in. Takes ten, fifteen years? Fine. We’re not just counting cash—we’re counting people.

And dialogue? Hell yes. Not yelling. Not online. Face to face. Like that meeting at the VFW hall last year—immigrant dads, old vets, pastors, teachers. Just talking. No agenda. One guy from Honduras said, “I walked 1,800 miles so my son wouldn’t die in the streets.” Man, that sat with me.

We don’t need agreement. We need understanding.

Because at the end of the day, fairness isn’t about numbers or borders. It’s about remembering that everyone’s carrying something. Some carry passports. Some carry trauma. Some carry hope so thin you can see through it.

And if this country means anything, it’s supposed to be a place where that hope gets a chance to grow.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character37_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Pauses a long time. Rubs his hands together like he’s cold, even in the sun]*

Complete openness? No. I respect the dream behind it—the “give everyone a chance”—but we’re not ready for that. Not with schools underfunded, hospitals overwhelmed, towns barely holding on. You can’t pour more water into a cracked bucket and expect it to hold.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s just stupid. And cruel. We’ve got an aging population. Farms need hands. Nursing homes are desperate. You shut the door completely, you don’t protect jobs—you break the damn system.

So what do I want?

A **mix**, like life always is.

First—**admit people based on job demand**, but *with rules*. Not just whatever boss says they “can’t find Americans.” Real proof. Try to hire locally first—advertise the job, pay a living wage, offer training. If *then* no one takes it after six weeks? Fine. Bring someone in—legally, documented, protected. Guest worker programs, yeah—but fix ’em so they ain’t indentured servitude. Let those workers change bosses. Let ’em sue if they’re cheated. And after ten years? A path to stay, if they want. Because people put down roots. You can’t keep kicking them out when they’ve raised kids here, paid taxes, mowed their lawn every Saturday like the rest of us.

Second—**set smart numerical limits**, not arbitrary ones. Not “50,000” because some politician picked a number. Base it on housing, infrastructure, regional needs. More in places with room and work, less where everything’s stretched thin. And leave room—*real room*—for refugees. Not just when it’s convenient. When it’s right. 25,000 a year? 50,000? Pick a number we can actually support—with housing, language classes, job matching. Don’t dump people in cities with nothing. Integrate ’em. Help ’em stand.

Third—**crack down hard on employers who exploit**. That’s the rot at the core. If you catch a company hiring undocumented workers to dodge wages and safety laws? Hit ’em where it hurts—fines, prison, lose your license. Make it riskier to cheat than to do right. That protects *everyone*—citizen and immigrant alike.

And fourth—**invest in our own people too**. Can’t ask folks in dying towns to welcome newcomers while their kids have no future. Expand trade schools. Bring back apprenticeships. Fund community colleges. Help people move, if they need to. Fairness goes both ways—if you expect tolerance, you gotta deliver opportunity.

Balance? It’s not about perfection. It’s about *fair motion*. Moving forward without leaving people behind.

Social integration doesn’t happen by accident. It happens when there’s space—space in the classroom, space in the clinic, space in the neighborhood. And when there’s dignity—for the man picking strawberries and the man who used to pick them before the machines came.

I want a policy that says: *We’ll open the door, but we’ll do it right. We’ll help you come, and we’ll help you belong. But we won’t let greed decide who gets in or how they live.*

That’s the America I still believe in. Not flawless. Not finished. But trying.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character37_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character37_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Sits quietly for a moment. Removes his glasses, wipes them slowly on his shirt—like he’s buying time to get it right]*

You know… I thought I knew what he’d say. I mean, we talked enough over the years—on porches, in parking lots, after church suppers. But actually *being* him today? Really stepping into those shoes again?

It brought back more than opinions.

It brought back the *weight* of it—the way he carried things. Not just anger or fear, but responsibility. Like he felt accountable—to the town, to the past, to people who never got a fair shake. Even when he was frustrated, even when he didn’t understand, he kept asking: “Is it fair?” That question never left him.

What surprised me? How much *mercy* was in him. I remembered the grumbling—the “why don’t they do it like we did?” stuff. But sitting here today, speaking as him, I heard something deeper: he wasn’t afraid of immigrants. He was afraid of being forgotten. Afraid that if everything changed, his life’s work—the decades of showing up, paying taxes, keeping quiet, doing right—wouldn’t count anymore.

And that fear? It’s real. But it doesn’t have to turn into hate. Today, I saw that in him more clearly—he wanted a world where *everyone* could belong, even if he wasn’t always sure how to make room.

As for me… well, I’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming. Maybe too idealistic. But walking in his boots today reminded me: you can’t just tell people to “get with the times.” You have to *see* them first. You have to acknowledge that change hurts—even when it’s necessary.

He wouldn’t want walls. But he’d want rules. Not to keep people out—but to make sure no one gets crushed along the way.

And maybe… maybe that’s where I’ve grown. I used to think fairness meant opening the door wide. Now I see—it also means making sure the floor doesn’t collapse when you do.

So thank you. This wasn’t just remembering him. It was listening—really listening—for the first time in years.

And I think… if he were here, he’d say the same thing I’m feeling now: We can do better. All of us. Together.
